title: "Frontier methods for digital soil mapping, evaluated honestly: a reproducible benchmark on real WoSIS Cerrado profiles"
author:
  - name: Hugo Rodrigues
    email: rodrigues.machado.hugo@gmail.com

abstract: |
  Digital soil mapping (DSM) has moved well beyond regression trees, yet the newer methods --- causal inference, physics-informed and generative deep learning, graph and quantum kernels --- are rarely evaluated against each other under a common, honest protocol, and their predictions are rarely reported with calibrated uncertainty. We present edaphos, an R framework that implements ten such method families behind a single posterior class so that any of them can be scored with the same diagnostics, and we use it to run a matched, spatially blocked benchmark of six methods on 1095 real World Soil Information Service (WoSIS) topsoil profiles over the Brazilian Cerrado. The result is deflationary and, we argue, useful: a plain ordinary-least-squares model on a directed-acyclic-graph (DAG)-selected covariate set is the most accurate and best-calibrated method in the comparison, and none of the five more elaborate pillars beats it on this task. We further show, on 3077 profiles, that backdoor adjustment yields robust associations with explicit sensitivity bounds rather than identified causal effects, and that instrumenting soil carbon with a trained foundation-model embedding produces very strong but invalid instruments (first-stage F $\approx$ 4630, Sargan p $\approx$ 3e-13) --- an empirical confirmation that a learned representation does not manufacture a valid instrument. We conclude that the contribution of a framework like edaphos is not a new best predictor but a reproducible, calibration-consistent apparatus for asking which method helps, and for reporting honestly when none does.

fmt <- function(x, d = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
CAU <- ex("causal_cerrado_real_v2.rds")
B6  <- ex("benchmark_wosis_6pilar.rds")
GAT <- ex("pilar10_gat_tuning.rds")

# Introduction

Digital soil mapping (DSM) predicts soil properties at unvisited locations from
spatially exhaustive covariates that proxy the soil-forming factors
[@McBratney2003]. The field's workhorse --- the random forest and its quantile
variants --- is accurate, fast and well understood, and a large recent literature
proposes to improve on it with methods borrowed from causal inference, deep
learning, and quantum machine learning. Two problems recur. First, these methods
are seldom compared under a common protocol: differences in cross-validation
scheme, ensemble budget, target transform and evaluation metric make published
gains hard to attribute to the method rather than the harness. Second, point
accuracy is reported far more often than calibrated uncertainty, even though a
soil map is used to make decisions under that uncertainty.

A third, more conceptual problem concerns causality. It is common in DSM to read
a covariate's importance in a predictive model as evidence that it *causes* the
soil property [@Wadoux2020]. Zhang and Wadoux [@Zhang2026causal] argue that
causal inference in DSM is possible only under conditions --- an explicit causal
model, causal sufficiency, and faithfulness --- that observational soil data
rarely satisfy, and that the generative, process-informed view of causation is
the one most compatible with those conditions.

This article makes three contributions, all reproducible from data bundled with
the software: (i) a single uncertainty-calibration interface that lets ten
method families be scored with the same diagnostics; (ii) a matched, spatially
blocked, uncertainty-aware benchmark of six methods on real WoSIS Cerrado
profiles, whose honest conclusion is that a DAG-informed OLS is the strongest
method here; and (iii) a causal analysis that reports backdoor-adjusted
associations with Cinelli--Hazlett robustness values, demonstrates confounding
directly, and reports a negative instrumental-variable result. We deliberately
foreground the negative findings: a framework that makes it easy to run a dozen
methods is only useful if it is equally easy to see when they do not help.

# Materials and methods

## Data

The benchmark uses `r B6$n_profiles` WoSIS [@Batjes2024wosis] topsoil (0--30 cm)
organic-carbon profiles over the Cerrado, retrieved from the ISRIC Web Feature
Service, with covariates extracted at each profile from WorldClim 2.1
[@Fick2017worldclim], SoilGrids [@Hengl2017soilgrids] and Copernicus fractional
tree cover. The causal analysis uses a larger draw of `r CAU$n_profiles`
profiles over the same region and covariate stack. Covariates are all
open-licensed and fetched from public endpoints, so the analysis is regenerable
from profile coordinates alone.

## A unified posterior and calibration interface

Every predictive method in edaphos returns, or can be coerced to, an
`edaphos_posterior`: a small object carrying a predictive sample (or mean and
standard deviation) for each target. A single routine then scores any of them
with the same measures --- the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), 90%
prediction-interval coverage (PICP) and mean width (MPIW), and a reliability
curve. This makes a like-for-like comparison across otherwise incompatible
methods possible: a random forest's quantiles, a Gibbs sampler's draws and a
diffusion model's samples are all reduced to the same currency.

## Methods compared

The benchmark compares one baseline and five frontier methods: **P1**, ordinary
least squares on the covariates in the backdoor adjustment set of an expert
pedogenetic DAG (the baseline); **P4**, a quantile random forest on the
principal components of a MoCo-v2 contrastive encoder trained on raster patches;
**P5**, a quantile random forest on the raw covariates; **P6**, quantum kernel
ridge regression using a ZZ-feature-map state-vector simulator; **P7**, a
Bayesian hierarchical spatial model fit by a Gibbs sampler; and **P10**, a graph
attention network over a *k*-nearest-neighbour co-location graph of profiles.

## Evaluation and causal protocol

All methods are evaluated on the same `r length(B6$folds)` spatially blocked
cross-validation folds, on the `r B6$response_scale` scale of organic carbon,
and scored against the achievable null --- each fold's training-fold mean, not the
global mean. Ensemble size is reported rather than forced equal. For the causal
analysis we build an expert Cerrado DAG, compute the minimal backdoor adjustment
set per exposure, estimate the adjusted association by OLS with a spatial block
bootstrap (500 resamples over 20 clusters), and pair every estimate with a
Cinelli--Hazlett robustness value (RV) [@CinelliHazlett2020]: the fraction of
residual variance an unobserved confounder would have to explain in both
exposure and outcome to drive the estimate to zero. We also attempt
instrumental-variable estimation, using the principal components of a
foundation-model embedding as instruments for precipitation, and test their
validity with the Sargan over-identification test.

# Results

## A DAG-informed OLS is the strongest method

```{r bench-table}
tb <- B6$cv_aggregate
show <- data.frame(
  Method = tb$method, RMSE = fmt(tb$rmse_mean, 3), `R2` = fmt(tb$r2_mean, 3),
  PICP90 = fmt(tb$picp90_mean, 3), MPIW90 = fmt(tb$mpiw90_mean, 3),
  CRPS = fmt(tb$crps_mean, 3), `Time (s)` = fmt(tb$elapsed_sum, 1),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(show, align = "lrrrrrr",
  caption = sprintf("Matched cross-pillar benchmark on %s WoSIS Cerrado profiles (%s spatially blocked folds, %s scale). RMSE and CRPS lower is better; R2 and PICP near 0.90 better.",
                    B6$n_profiles, length(B6$folds), B6$response_scale))
```

Ordinary least squares on the DAG-selected covariates has the lowest RMSE
(`r fmt(min(B6$cv_aggregate$rmse_mean),3)`) and the highest coefficient of
determination (`r fmt(max(B6$cv_aggregate$r2_mean),3)`), and its calibration
(PICP `r fmt(B6$cv_aggregate$picp90_mean[1],3)`) is among the best (Table 1). The
random forest is a close second. The three deep or exotic methods --- foundation
embeddings, graph attention, and the quantum kernel --- sit progressively lower,
and all three fall below the achievable null ($R^2 < 0$): on these spatially
blocked folds they explain less than predicting the training mean. The quantum
kernel is both least accurate and, at
`r fmt(B6$cv_aggregate$elapsed_sum[nrow(B6$cv_aggregate)],0)` s, several hundred
times slower than the baseline (Fig 1). The spread among the top methods is
small relative to the fold-to-fold standard deviation
($\approx$ `r fmt(mean(B6$cv_aggregate$rmse_sd),2)` RMSE), so we do not over-read
the ordering beyond its headline: elaboration did not pay here.

```{r bench-plot, fig.cap = "Accuracy (RMSE, lower better) against variance explained (R2 vs the training-fold mean). The DAG-informed OLS (filled) is the most accurate; every more elaborate method sits down and to the left, and three fall below the achievable null."}
tb <- B6$cv_aggregate
op <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1, 1))
plot(tb$rmse_mean, tb$r2_mean, type = "n",
     xlab = "RMSE (log1p g/kg, lower better)",
     ylab = expression(R^2~"vs training-fold mean"))
abline(h = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey60")
pch <- ifelse(grepl("OLS", tb$method), 19, 21)
points(tb$rmse_mean, tb$r2_mean, pch = pch, cex = 1.6, bg = "white",
       col = "#2c3e50", lwd = 1.5)
text(tb$rmse_mean, tb$r2_mean, sub(" .*", "", tb$method), pos = 4, cex = 0.8)
par(op)
```

When tuned under nested cross-validation (`r GAT$n_profiles` profiles; outer
folds never used for tuning), the graph attention network reaches a pooled
Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency of
`r fmt(GAT$pooled$nse_vs_training_fold_mean[1],3)` against the tuned forest's
`r fmt(GAT$pooled$nse_vs_training_fold_mean[2],3)` --- an edge whose 95%
block-bootstrap confidence interval,
[`r fmt(GAT$boot_diff_ci[1],3)`, `r fmt(GAT$boot_diff_ci[2],3)`], spans zero
(P(GAT ahead) = `r fmt(GAT$p_gat_beats_qrf,3)`). The attention mechanism is thus
competitive with, not superior to, a random forest.

## Causal inference: robust associations, and why identification is hard

```{r causal-table}
e <- CAU$effects
lab <- c(wc_bio_12 = "Precipitation (per mm)", wc_bio_01 = "Temperature (per degC)",
         wc_landcover_trees = "Tree cover (per 0-1)", soilgrids_clay = "Clay (per %)")
show <- data.frame(
  Exposure = lab[e$exposure], `Naive` = fmt(e$beta_naive, 3),
  `Adjusted` = fmt(e$beta_adj, 3),
  `95% CI` = sprintf("[%s, %s]", fmt(e$ci_lo, 3), fmt(e$ci_hi, 3)),
  Sig. = ifelse(e$signif, "yes", "no"), RV = fmt(e$RV, 2), check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(show, align = "lrrccr",
  caption = sprintf("Backdoor-adjusted associations on %s WoSIS Cerrado profiles (g/kg topsoil carbon per unit exposure). RV: Cinelli-Hazlett robustness value.", CAU$n_profiles))
```

Two associations are robust and mechanistically sensible (Table 2):
precipitation and clay content both raise topsoil carbon, are distinguishable
from zero, and would each need an unobserved confounder explaining about 16--18% of
residual variance in both exposure and outcome to overturn. The temperature
association carries the expected negative sign but is not distinguishable from
zero. The tree-cover row is instructive: its naive association
(`r fmt(e$beta_naive[e$exposure=='wc_landcover_trees'],2)`) all but vanishes
after adjusting for climate
(`r fmt(e$beta_adj[e$exposure=='wc_landcover_trees'],2)`, interval spanning zero,
RV `r fmt(e$RV[e$exposure=='wc_landcover_trees'],3)`) --- the raw signal was
largely shared climatic ancestry. This is exactly the confounding that
Zhang and Wadoux [@Zhang2026causal] warn is misread as causal, shown directly on
real data.

Backdoor adjustment identifies an effect only under causal sufficiency.
Instrumental variables promise identification under a different assumption --- that
an instrument affects the outcome only through the exposure. We trained a real
MoCo-v2 foundation encoder (`r CAU$encoder$channels` covariate channels,
`r format(CAU$encoder$tiles, big.mark=',')` tiles,
`r format(CAU$encoder$epochs, big.mark=',')` epochs) and used the principal
components of its per-profile landscape embedding as instruments for
precipitation. The instruments are extremely relevant --- a first-stage $F$ of
`r round(CAU$iv$first_stage_F)`, far above the usual threshold of 10 --- yet they
decisively fail the Sargan over-identification test
($\chi^2$(`r CAU$iv$sargan_df`) = `r fmt(CAU$iv$sargan_stat,1)`,
$p \approx$ `r formatC(CAU$iv$sargan_p, format='e', digits=0)`). A learned
landscape representation encodes climate, terrain, soil and vegetation together,
so it reaches carbon through many paths and violates the exclusion restriction.
Even a powerful learned representation does not manufacture a valid instrument;
we report the failed test, not a headline effect.

# Discussion

The benchmark's conclusion --- that a DAG-informed OLS is the strongest method,
and that three of five frontier pillars fall below the achievable null ---
deserves care in either direction. It does not show that deep learning cannot
work in DSM; it shows that on about 1000 point profiles with a handful of coarse
covariates, the sample and signal are too small for high-capacity models to
express an advantage, and that a linear model on well-chosen covariates is hard
to beat. This is a common finding for tabular problems at this scale, and it is
precisely the kind of result that a matched, uncertainty-aware protocol surfaces
and an accuracy-only, single-method report hides. The calibration columns make
the same point from another angle: the quantum kernel's narrow intervals buy the
worst coverage, an overconfidence a point-accuracy table would never reveal.

The causal results carry the second message. Backdoor adjustment on an explicit
DAG is a legitimate and useful tool --- it recovered a robust precipitation and
clay signal and exposed the tree-cover association as mostly confounding --- but
the honest object it returns is an adjusted association with a sensitivity
bound, not an identified causal effect. The negative IV result sharpens this:
the most tempting modern shortcut to identification, a learned representation as
instrument, is the wrong tool, because the property that makes an embedding a
good predictor (it captures everything) is the property that makes it an invalid
instrument (it violates exclusion).

The limitations are inherent to the design. A single biome, about 1000--3000 profiles,
and coarse covariates are a hard setting for high-capacity methods; a larger,
denser survey with fine-resolution covariates might let the foundation encoder or
graph network express structure they cannot here, and the framework is built to
make that re-test a one-line change of data. The benchmark scores prediction, not
the process-informed generative modelling that Zhang and Wadoux
[@Zhang2026causal] identify as the most defensible route to causal claims.

# Conclusion

We have presented a reproducible framework that reduces ten families of DSM
method to a common posterior-and-calibration currency, and used it to run a
matched, honest benchmark whose lesson is deflationary: on real WoSIS Cerrado
profiles a DAG-informed ordinary-least-squares model is the most accurate and
best-calibrated method, and no more elaborate pillar beats it. The value we
claim is not a new best predictor but the apparatus --- and the discipline --- for
finding out which method helps, reporting calibrated uncertainty, and stating
plainly when the answer is "none of the new ones, here." The same apparatus
delivered a robust causal association analysis with explicit sensitivity bounds
and a clean negative instrumental-variable result, operationalising the caution
that causal identification from observational soil data is hard.

# Data and code availability {#dataavail .unnumbered}

edaphos and all bundled result data are available at
https://github.com/HugoMachadoRodrigues/edaphos. Soil profiles are from WoSIS
(ISRIC, CC-BY-4.0); covariates from WorldClim 2.1, SoilGrids and Copernicus. The
retrieval and analysis pipeline is in `data-raw/`, and every figure in this
manuscript is reproduced by the `edaphos-paper` package vignette from the shipped
data.
